name: Contrast Effect
description: Judgments of an option, person, or price shift depending on what was seen just before or beside it, so the same target can feel better or worse by comparison. Relative context changes evaluation even when the focal item itself is unchanged.
design_relevance_note: Highly relevant to pricing ladders, merchandising, benchmark dashboards, and side-by-side comparison UI: adjacent context can make the same plan, feature, or metric feel cheap, premium, weak, or strong.
myth_risk_note: Well-demonstrated in the specific contexts tested (hedonic contrast, conditioning) but the term spans a broad family of related phenomena across domains; the popular umbrella label may overgeneralize beyond what any single study tests.
prevalence_note: Well known in pricing, merchandising, conversion-rate-optimization, and persuasion-design circles, even if less central in general UX curricula.

findings.description: Across five experiments, local processing reliably produced contrast in social judgment while global processing produced assimilation, showing that the evaluation of a target shifts systematically with comparison context and processing mode rather than remaining fully absolute.
findings.source_title: The effect of global versus local processing styles on assimilation versus contrast in social judgment.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: Marsh & Hau's 26-country academic self-concept study
applications.description: Testing nationally representative samples of roughly 4,000 15-year-olds in each of 26 countries (total N = 103,558), researchers found that attending a higher-achieving school consistently lowered students' own academic self-concept, compared to equally able students at a lower-achieving school -- the 'big-fish-little-pond effect,' a direct application of social comparison and contrast to educational settings. The negative effect held in all 26 countries studied, with a consistent average effect size.
applications.ethical_note: A large, rigorous social-comparison research finding with no persuasion or product-design angle -- relevant as a caution wherever a product surfaces relative-performance comparisons (leaderboards, cohort benchmarking in learning apps) that could similarly lower a user's self-assessment relative to context rather than absolute skill.
